Key Concepts

What these mean in practice

SDLC — Software Development Life Cycle

A step-by-step process that professional software teams follow to build reliable software. Instead of jumping straight into coding, you plan, design, build, test, and then release — in that order.

01  Requirements — what does the app need to do?
02  Design — ER diagrams, system architecture
03  Development — write the PHP / MySQL code
04  Testing — unit tests, validation checks
05  Deployment — launch and monitor
Used in: Online Shopping Portal project
KPI Tracking — Key Performance Indicators

KPIs are specific numbers a business watches to know if things are going well. Tracking them means collecting that data daily, building dashboards, and alerting the team when something is off target.

📦  Inventory accuracy — TC (Tally Count) vs system records
🚚  TMS shipment status — inbound/outbound on schedule?
🚪  Gating accuracy — correct entries logged at facility gates?
⚠️  Discrepancies per shift — errors flagged and resolved
✅  Data fidelity — 100% accuracy across all large trackers
Tools used: MS Excel · TMS · Gating · TC · Large Trackers

Projects

Things I've built

🛒
Online Shopping Portal

A secure, full-stack eCommerce web application with multi-role authentication for Admin, Distributor, Stockist, and Customer. Features real-time product management, live order tracking, and automated inventory updates.

Built using the Waterfall SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle) — a structured engineering process where each phase is completed before the next begins: Requirements gathering → System Design (ER diagrams) → Coding → Testing (unit tests + validation) → Deployment. This ensured the project was planned properly before a single line of code was written, resulting in fewer bugs and a more maintainable codebase.

PHP MySQL JavaScript HTML/CSS SDLC Multi-role Auth
📊
Logistics Analytics Dashboard

Built and maintained daily operational reports and large trackers at Flipkart using MS Excel, TMS (Transport Management System), Gating, and TC (Tally Count) tools.

These trackers monitor KPIs (Key Performance Indicators) — specific numbers that show whether the warehouse is hitting its targets. Examples include: inventory accuracy rate (are stock counts correct?), discrepancies flagged per shift (how many errors caught via TC?), gating entry/exit accuracy, and TMS shipment status. Operations leads use these numbers every shift to make decisions about staffing, routing, and priorities.
